title: Roadmap 16: System design process and LLD
seriesDescription: Topic-by-topic quizzes that follow the backend interview roadmap: language core, concurrency, DSA habits, web frameworks, data access, databases, messaging, resilience, security, testing, system design, and LLM/agent engineering.
description: The interview framework, back-of-envelope estimates, rate limiter and auth service design, multi-tenancy, reconciliation pipelines, and low-level design basics.
source: Interview roadmap study plan (Java/Spring Boot and Python/FastAPI)

questions.prompt: True or false: a strong system design answer starts by drawing the high-level boxes, and clarifying requirements can wait until later.

options.text: True
options.why: Boxes drawn first usually solve the wrong problem.

options.text: False
options.why: Correct: clarify functional and non-functional requirements first, then estimate, define the API and data model, draw the design and deep dive.

questions.explanation: A solid order: requirements, estimates, API, data model, high-level design, deep dive, trade-offs and failure modes.

questions.prompt: 10 million daily active users each make 20 read requests per day. Roughly what is the average read QPS?

options.text: About 2,300 requests per second.
options.why: Right: 200 million per day divided by 86,400 seconds.

options.text: About 23,000 requests per second.
options.why: Off by a factor of ten.

options.text: About 230 requests per second.
options.why: Too low by a factor of ten.

options.text: About 200,000 requests per second.
options.why: That divides by about 1,000 instead of the seconds in a day.

questions.explanation: Use 100,000 seconds per day as a shortcut, then state a peak factor (often 2-3x) and size for the peak.

questions.prompt: An API runs on twelve gateway instances and must allow 100 requests per minute per API key overall. Where should the counters live?

options.text: In shared Redis, updated atomically with INCR plus expiry.
options.why: Right: all instances see one count and updates cannot race.

options.text: In each instance's memory, with each instance allowing 100 per minute.
options.why: The real limit becomes up to 1,200 per minute.

options.text: In a relational row locked with SELECT FOR UPDATE on every request.
options.why: Correct but makes the database a bottleneck on the hot path.

options.text: In the client, which promises to stay under its limit.
options.why: Clients are untrusted and cannot enforce limits.

questions.explanation: Decide the failure mode too: fail open (allow) or fail closed if Redis is down. Return 429 with a Retry-After header.

questions.prompt: True or false: a token bucket allows short bursts up to the bucket size while enforcing the long-run average refill rate.

options.text: True
options.why: Correct: spare tokens accumulate up to the capacity and can be spent at once.

options.text: False
options.why: That describes the bucket; a strict per-second limit does not allow bursts.

questions.explanation: Sliding window counters give smoother limits at the cost of more state or an approximation; fixed windows allow double bursts at window edges.

questions.prompt: Select all that apply. Which choices suit a JWT-based authentication service?

options.text: Issue short-lived access tokens and keep refresh tokens revocable and rotated.
options.why: Right: limits the damage of a leaked token.

options.text: Sign with an asymmetric key and publish public keys via a JWKS endpoint.
options.why: Right: services verify tokens without holding the signing secret.

options.text: Include a key id (kid) in the header so signing keys can be rotated.
options.why: Right: old and new keys can both verify during rotation.

options.text: Issue 30 day access tokens so that revocation is never needed.
options.why: A stolen token would stay valid for 30 days.

options.text: Share the signing secret with every consuming service so each can issue tokens.
options.why: Widens the blast radius of a leaked secret.

questions.explanation: Expect follow-ups on logout, password change and revocation: server-side sessions, a denylist, or short expiry.

questions.prompt: In a shared-schema multi-tenant SaaS, what best prevents one tenant from reading another's rows?

options.text: Take the tenant from the verified token and enforce it with row-level security.
options.why: Right: developers cannot forget a filter.

options.text: Ask each developer to add WHERE tenant_id = ? to every single query they write.
options.why: One forgotten clause is a data breach.

options.text: Read the tenant id from a request body field that the client sends.
options.why: Any client can send another tenant's id.

options.text: Hide the tenant ids by using long random numbers in the URLs.
options.why: Obscurity is not authorisation.

questions.explanation: Mention the trade-offs of schema per tenant and database per tenant, and plan to move very large tenants to dedicated resources.

questions.prompt: A nightly job reconciles SAP documents with the warehouse. About 0.5% of records mismatch, mostly SAP postings made after the extract cutoff. What is the best fix?

options.text: Match on business keys and re-check unmatched records in later runs first.
options.why: Right: late data resolves itself without hiding true gaps.

options.text: Widen the amount tolerance until the mismatch count looks acceptable to the business.
options.why: Hides real discrepancies and does not fix missing rows.

options.text: Delete warehouse rows that SAP does not contain at the extract cutoff time.
options.why: Destroys data that arrives correctly one run later.

options.text: Compare only row counts per table and ignore individual records.
options.why: Equal counts can hide offsetting missing and extra rows.

questions.explanation: Reconcile with business keys, small tolerances for rounding, per-status reports and an aging window for late data.

questions.prompt: Select all that apply. Which statements about low-level design answers are correct?

options.text: An LRU cache gets O(1) get and put from a hash map plus a doubly linked list.
options.why: Right: the map finds nodes and the list reorders them in constant time.

options.text: In a thread-safe LRU cache, get also needs protection because it reorders the list.
options.why: Right: reads mutate recency order.

options.text: A parking lot should model vehicles, spots and tickets, with pricing as a swappable strategy.
options.why: Right: pricing rules change often.

options.text: A singly linked list with no map is enough for O(1) LRU lookups.
options.why: Finding a key would require scanning the list.

options.text: The parking lot should hard-code pricing in its entry method because rates never change.
options.why: Rates do change; hard-coding breaks the open/closed principle.

questions.explanation: Clarify requirements, list entities and relationships, then pick patterns only where they remove a real problem.
